column2:
Your team uses Claude Code for multi-file refactors that routinely run two to three hours. Engineers currently type the task and let Claude start editing immediately; in about a third of these sessions Claude's approach diverges from what the engineer intended, and they spend 40-plus minutes reverting and re-prompting after the fact.

What working habit would most reduce this cleanup time?

A. Switch the sessions to a larger-context model so Claude retains the engineer's original intent for the full run.
B. Add a CLAUDE.md rule stating that Claude must describe its intended approach before editing any file.
C. Start each refactor in plan mode, read the proposed plan thoroughly, and iterate on it before approving execution.
D. Break every refactor into single-file tasks and dispatch each one to a fresh session.
column3:
Correct Answer: C. Option C targets the root cause: in plan mode Claude researches in read-only mode and hands you a plan to review, and iterating on a plan is much faster than letting Claude run and cleaning up afterward — a thorough, actually-read plan means fewer surprises during execution. Option A misdiagnoses the problem; the divergence is a scoping failure, not a context-capacity failure. Option B relies on probabilistic instruction-following and produces no reviewable artifact you can iterate on before code changes. Option D destroys the cross-file context a refactor depends on and multiplies coordination overhead across sessions.

column2:
Four hours into a Claude Code session, you finished a lengthy debugging detour 90 minutes ago and are now implementing a --version flag. The context window is nearly full. The last time you ran a bare /compact in a similar session, the summary kept the debugging details, dropped the implementation decisions you cared about, and Claude drifted.

How should you free up context while keeping Claude on track?

A. Run /compact with no arguments; the summarizer automatically weights recent work over older detours.
B. Run /compact followed by instructions naming what matters, such as /compact Focus on the --version flag implementation.
C. Switch to a model with a larger context window and continue the session without compacting.
D. Start a fresh session and re-explain the task from scratch to guarantee a clean context.
column3:
Correct Answer: B. Option B uses compaction's steering wheel: anything written after the command shapes what the summary keeps, so the --version work survives and the stale debugging detour is dropped. Option A repeats exactly the failure described — an undirected summary gives you no control over what gets kept. Option C postpones the problem and leaves the irrelevant debugging content in context competing for attention. Option D throws away all accumulated, still-relevant context and costs significant re-explanation time when a directed summary would have preserved it.

column2:
Fifty minutes into a feature build, you realize Claude committed to the wrong architecture about 20 minutes ago and has since edited nine files on that basis. Engineers on your team usually respond by prompting corrections such as 'undo all of that and go back to the event-based approach', which typically takes another half hour and leaves stray code behind.

What is the most reliable way to get both the code and the conversation back on track?

A. Ask Claude to revert its changes and restate the intended architecture in one detailed corrective prompt.
B. Use git checkout to restore the nine files, then continue working in the existing conversation.
C. Kill the session and start over so no trace of the wrong architecture remains anywhere.
D. Double-tap escape to open the rewind menu and restore both code and conversation at the checkpoint before the wrong turn.
column3:
Correct Answer: D. Option D uses what checkpoints are for: every user prompt creates one, and restoring code and conversation together removes both the bad edits and the conversational context that keeps steering Claude toward the abandoned architecture. Option A is the slow pattern the team already suffers from — probabilistic cleanup that leaves strays. Option B rolls back the files but leaves 20 minutes of wrong-architecture discussion in context, so Claude is likely to drift back. Option C discards the 30 minutes of good context that preceded the wrong turn when a checkpoint restore would have kept it.

• Interactive mode (/compact, shortcuts)

column2:
Your session began with 90 minutes of codebase exploration and environment setup before implementation started. You are now deep in implementation, the context window is at 85%, and the recent implementation turns contain decisions Claude must keep in full detail.

Which action frees context while preserving the implementation detail?

A. Open the rewind menu and choose 'Summarize up to here' at the checkpoint where implementation began.
B. Open the rewind menu and choose 'Restore conversation' at the checkpoint where implementation began.
C. Run a bare /compact so the entire conversation, setup and implementation alike, is summarized.
D. Continue without compacting and rely on the model to attend to recent turns over older ones.
column3:
Correct Answer: A. Option A is the designed move for a long setup phase: 'Summarize up to here' compresses everything before the chosen checkpoint while keeping everything after it — the implementation turns — intact. Option B does not compress anything; restoring the conversation at that checkpoint deletes the implementation turns you need to keep. Option C summarizes the implementation detail along with the setup, risking exactly the decisions you need verbatim. Option D leaves the window filling toward overflow while 90 minutes of stale setup keeps competing for attention.

column2:
You want Claude to keep working across turns on a billing module until it is genuinely done, rather than stopping the first time it thinks it is finished. A teammate proposes running /goal the billing dashboard looks correct and users are happy with it.

What should you tell the teammate?

A. The condition is too brief; expand it with a detailed description of the dashboard's intended design so the evaluator has more to compare against.
B. Rephrase it as something checkable from Claude's own output, such as /goal all tests in src/billing pass and the type checker reports zero errors.
C. /goal accepts only a single condition per session, so split it: run /goal the dashboard looks correct now and handle user satisfaction in a second session.
D. Keep the condition, but have Claude report a confidence score at the end of each turn and treat 95% or higher as the signal that the goal is met.
column3:
Correct Answer: B. Option B states the one hard constraint on goals: the fast evaluator confirms completion only from the session transcript, so 'done' must be phrased as something Claude's own output can demonstrate, like test results or type-checker output — 'looks correct and users are happy' produces nothing checkable. Option A adds words without adding verifiability; a longer unverifiable condition is still unverifiable. Option C invents a limit that does not exist and would not make the condition checkable anyway. Option D substitutes self-reported confidence for evidence, and a model's confidence score is not a reliable completion signal.

column2:
After Claude pushes a branch, your team wants the session to watch the CI pipeline — runs take 10 to 20 minutes — and triage any failures once the run finishes. Today engineers sit at the terminal re-asking 'is CI done yet?' every few minutes.

Which Claude Code capability fits this job?

A. Set /goal CI passes; the goal evaluator will poll the pipeline until the condition is met.
B. Add a CLAUDE.md rule instructing Claude to always wait for CI to finish before ending its turn.
C. Raise the session's turn budget so Claude keeps retrying the CI status check until the run completes.
D. Start a loop that runs a status-check prompt on an interval so Claude acts when the CI state changes.
column3:
Correct Answer: D. Option D is what loop exists for: it runs a prompt on a fixed or self-paced interval between turns, which is exactly the shape of polling external state like CI or a deploy and reacting when it changes. Option A misunderstands goal — the evaluator only reads the transcript to confirm a completion condition from output Claude produced; it does not poll external systems on a schedule. Option B is a probabilistic instruction, and an instruction cannot make a turn wait on an external event. Option C burns turns on blind retries, automating the team's current busywork rather than replacing it with an interval-driven check.

column2:
Three feature refactors are due this week, so your team runs three concurrent Claude Code sessions against the same repository. In roughly 30% of runs, one session overwrites files another session just edited. Each feature's dev server also needs a git-ignored .env.local file to boot, and security policy forbids committing it.

Which TWO changes let the three sessions run in parallel reliably? (Select TWO.)

A. Run each session in its own git worktree so every agent works on an independent file tree.
B. Serialize the work into a single session and queue the three refactors one after another.
C. Add a .worktreeinclude file at the repo root listing .env.local so it is copied into each worktree.
D. Commit .env.local to the repository so every checkout automatically includes it.
column3:
Correct Answer: A and C. Options A and C are both required. Worktrees (A) end the clobbering: instead of two steering wheels in one car, each session gets its own independent file tree, and clean worktrees are removed automatically when a session exits. But a worktree does not contain git-ignored files, so the dev servers would fail to boot; a .worktreeinclude file (C) lists exactly those files — env files, local config — to copy into each worktree. Option B eliminates the conflicts by abandoning the parallelism the deadline requires. Option D puts secrets into version control, which policy forbids and which .worktreeinclude makes unnecessary.

column2:
Your project CLAUDE.md contains 'IMPORTANT: never push directly to main.' Over the last month of heavy agent use, Claude pushed to main twice out of roughly 200 sessions, each time triggering an incident review.

What is the right fix?

A. Move the rule to the first line of CLAUDE.md and repeat it again at the bottom so it cannot be missed.
B. Add few-shot examples to CLAUDE.md demonstrating the correct branch-and-PR workflow.
C. Enforce the rule with a PreToolUse hook that blocks any push to main, and keep CLAUDE.md for softer conventions.
D. Reword it to 'YOU MUST NEVER push to main' and duplicate it in your user-level CLAUDE.md so it loads in every session.
column3:
Correct Answer: C. Option C matches the surface to the rule: CLAUDE.md is guidance, not enforced configuration, and 99% compliance is not good enough for an action with incident-level consequences. A PreToolUse hook is code that runs before the action and blocks it even when Claude tries it — real enforcement instead of a polite request. Options A, B, and D are all escalations of prompt-only enforcement; they may lower the failure rate but remain probabilistic, and a hard line that must never be crossed cannot depend on instruction-following. Option D additionally duplicates a project rule into personal scope, where it does nothing for teammates' sessions.

column2:
Your project CLAUDE.md has grown to 700 lines mixing style conventions, long task-specific reference material, and a rule that Claude must never run destructive database commands against the shared staging environment. Adherence has degraded across the board, and last week Claude ran a destructive command against staging anyway.

Which TWO changes most directly address these failures? (Select TWO.)

A. Mark every rule in the file IMPORTANT so that none of them gets deprioritized.
B. Move the destructive-command rule into a PreToolUse hook that blocks matching commands before they run.
C. Split the 700 lines across ten files pulled in with @ imports to reduce the context the file consumes.
D. Cut the file down to the conventions that matter and move task-specific reference material into skills that load only when they apply.
column3:
Correct Answer: B and D. Options B and D fix the two distinct failures. The staging rule is a hard line, and CLAUDE.md is guidance that Claude can fail to follow; a PreToolUse hook (B) blocks the action deterministically even on runs nobody is watching. The adherence collapse is a length problem: every line competes with every other line for attention, so trimming the file and scoping task-specific material into skills (D) makes the remaining rules more reliably followed. Option A is emphasis inflation — if every rule shouts, nothing stands out. Option C only reorganizes: imports are expanded inline at launch, so everything still loads and the attention competition is unchanged.

column2:
A line in your CLAUDE.md reads 'Follow best practices for API routes.' Code review still flags misplaced route files in about 4 of every 10 Claude-generated PRs, and your own engineers disagree about what the rule actually requires.

How should the rule be rewritten?

A. Make it specific and checkable, such as 'Put new API routes in src/api/handlers, one file per route.'
B. Prefix it with IMPORTANT so it wins the competition for Claude's attention.
C. Replace it with a PreToolUse hook that rejects any edit whose diff violates best practices.
D. Import the team's full 30-page style guide into CLAUDE.md so best practices are completely defined.
column3:
Correct Answer: A. Option A clears the bar every rule should meet: you can look at the result and immediately tell whether it was followed. If you cannot check a rule, neither can Claude — vagueness, not attention, is why this rule fails; even the humans disagree on its meaning. Option B raises the priority of a rule that still does not say what to do. Option C cannot be built: a hook is deterministic code, and 'best practices' is undefined, so there is nothing concrete for it to check — the phrasing is the failure, not the enforcement. Option D loads a wall of competing text, and the longer the file, the less reliably Claude follows any single rule.

column2:
Your CLAUDE.md says 'Don't use default exports.' Claude complies with the ban but improvises the alternative: across 15 recent files, some use named exports, some re-export through index files, and two fall back to CommonJS module.exports, forcing rework.

What change makes the rule land consistently?

A. Move the rule into its own imported file so it no longer competes with the rules around it.
B. Add three few-shot code examples to CLAUDE.md demonstrating named exports in context.
C. Escalate the wording to 'YOU MUST not use default exports' to raise its priority.
D. Rephrase it to name the replacement: 'Use named exports, not default exports.'
column3:
Correct Answer: D. Option D closes the door the current rule leaves open: a ban without a named replacement invites any alternative, which is exactly the improvisation you are seeing. Naming what to do instead leaves nothing to misinterpret. Option A reorganizes the file but changes nothing about the rule's ambiguity — and imported files are expanded inline anyway. Option B spends tokens demonstrating what one precise sentence can state directly. Option C raises the priority of the prohibition, but Claude is already honoring the prohibition; the failure is in what to do instead, which stronger emphasis on the ban cannot supply.

column2:
Over six months, engineers added IMPORTANT or YOU MUST to any rule Claude ignored; 31 of the 40 rules in your project CLAUDE.md now carry that emphasis. This month Claude repeatedly violated the two rules with real consequences: migrations must ship with a rollback plan, and new endpoints must document their auth requirements.

How should the team restore the effectiveness of emphasis?

A. Move the two critical rules to the top of the file, since rules earlier in the file override later ones.
B. Strip the emphasis from routine rules and spend it only on the two or three rules that hurt most when broken.
C. Upgrade the two critical rules to all-caps with the warning repeated in consecutive lines.
D. Convert all 40 rules into PreToolUse hooks so that none of them depends on Claude's attention.
column3:
Correct Answer: B. Option B applies the principle that emphasis is a budget: IMPORTANT and YOU MUST raise a rule's priority only relative to the quieter rules around it, so when 31 of 40 rules shout, the two that matter get no lift at all. Reserving emphasis for the consequential few restores the contrast that makes it work. Option A relies on an ordering mechanism the file does not have; position is not the lever, relative emphasis is. Option C continues the same inflation arms race that caused the failure. Option D is over-engineered: most of the 40 are soft conventions with no deterministic check a hook could run, and the fix for diluted emphasis is spending it more selectively, not abandoning guidance altogether.

column2:
You are two weeks into a solo refactor on a long-lived branch and want Claude to hold a set of interim architectural decisions in mind every session. The decisions would confuse the other 11 engineers if they applied to their sessions, and they are irrelevant to your other projects.

Where should these instructions live?

A. In local memory (CLAUDE.local.md), which is ignored by git and applies only to you in this repository.
B. In the shared project CLAUDE.md, prefixed with a note that only sessions on the refactor branch should apply them.
C. In your user-level CLAUDE.md, so the decisions follow you without touching the repository.
D. In a skill whose description mentions the refactor, so the decisions load only when they seem relevant.
column3:
Correct Answer: A. Option A is exactly what the local memory location is for: all four locations (managed policy, user, project, local) load together, and local is the one scoped to just you in just this repository — the course's example is precisely holding your own architectural decisions during a refactor. Option B ships your interim decisions to all 12 engineers and then hopes each session correctly ignores a disclaimer, polluting shared context either way. Option C has the wrong scope in the other direction: user memory follows you into every project on your machine. Option D turns standing per-repo context into a conditionally triggered procedure; these decisions must be in play every session, not only when a description happens to match.

References:
• Manage Claude's memory (CLAUDE.md)

column2:
To reduce Claude's startup context, a teammate split your 900-line project CLAUDE.md into six files referenced with @.claude/conventions/... imports. The next session's context usage at launch is unchanged, and the teammate files a bug report.

What should you tell them?

A. Imports load lazily when Claude first needs them, and the launch context meter reports reserved rather than actual usage, so the change did work.
B. The @ import syntax requires absolute paths; relative paths such as @.claude/conventions/... silently fall back to inlining every file at launch.
C. Imports expand inline at launch, so they organize content without shrinking it; move task-specific material into skills, which load only when they apply.
D. Nest the six files behind a single index file that imports the others, so only the index is read at launch and the rest load when referenced.
column3:
Correct Answer: C. Option C describes the actual mechanism: when Claude launches, imported files are expanded inline right where they are referenced — imports keep a big file tidy, but everything still loads up front, so the meter is telling the truth. Actually shrinking always-loaded context means relocating task-specific material to a surface that loads on demand, such as skills. Options A and B invent behaviors the feature does not have; imports are neither lazy nor path-sensitive in that way. Option D changes nothing, because imports expand recursively — the index pulls in all six files at launch just as before.

column2:
Last quarter, 3 of the 20 Claude-assisted refactors your team shipped passed CI only because test assertions had been quietly loosened during the refactor so failing tests would pass. Whether anyone re-checked the diff depended on the individual engineer remembering to ask.

What change most directly closes this gap?

A. A Stop hook that runs the full test suite after every refactor and refuses to let the turn end until every test passes.
B. A verification skill that runs the suite, reads the diff to confirm no test was loosened, and reports pass or fail with evidence.
C. A CLAUDE.md rule, marked IMPORTANT, stating 'Always double-check your work and confirm the tests are still sound before finishing.'
D. Having Claude self-report a confidence score for each refactor so reviewers spend their diff-reading time on the low-confidence ones.
column3:
Correct Answer: B. Option B addresses both failure modes at once. The problem is not tests failing to run — it is tests being weakened so they pass, plus checking that depends on human memory. A skill triggers itself when its description matches the situation and walks the same steps every time, and the decisive step is reading the diff to confirm no test was loosened; green alone is not 'done'. Option A guarantees the tests run and pass, but a loosened test passes — the one failure this team actually has is invisible to it. Option C is a vague instruction with no procedure behind it; emphasis raises its priority but still does not say how to check, and it competes for attention with everything else in the file. Option D routes review effort by self-reported confidence, which has no reliable relationship to whether assertions were weakened.

column2:
Your team's database-migration skill is a single SKILL.md of about 1,100 lines: a 12-step procedure, a full schema-conventions reference, and a 200-line shell script pasted as a code block that Claude is told to copy into a file and run. Every invocation loads all of it into context.

How should the skill folder be restructured?

A. Split it into three separate skills — procedure, schema reference, and script — each with its own description so every part loads and triggers independently.
B. Move the whole skill into the project CLAUDE.md behind an @ import so it loads once at launch instead of on every invocation.
C. Condense the procedure, the reference, and the script's steps into summary bullets so the entire SKILL.md fits in far fewer tokens.
D. Keep the procedure in a lean SKILL.md, move the schema conventions to a linked reference.md, and ship the script as an executable file in the folder.
column3:
Correct Answer: D. Option D uses what the skill folder is for: the entry file stays short and describes what to do, a reference.md linked from it holds the heavy material and is read only when that depth is needed, and scripts placed in the folder are executed rather than loaded, so the skill carries its own tooling at no context cost. Option A fragments one procedure across three trigger surfaces, and reference text or a script is not itself a task that should fire independently. Option B moves task-specific material into always-loaded memory — the opposite of scoping, and a burden on every session. Option C sacrifices detail the migration genuinely needs when relocating it would have kept both the depth and the lean entry point.

column2:
Your pre-release checks skill produces roughly 8,000 tokens of build logs and test output per run. Engineers invoke it several times during long sessions, and after two or three invocations the main conversation fills with stale logs and Claude starts losing track of the feature work.

Which frontmatter change fixes this?

A. Add context: fork so the skill runs in its own forked subagent context instead of the main conversation.
B. Add allowed-tools limiting the skill to read-only tools so it generates less output.
C. Add argument-hint so engineers can pass a flag that suppresses the log output.
D. Add disable-model-invocation: true so the skill runs less frequently during long sessions.
column3:
Correct Answer: A. Option A solves the actual problem: with context: fork, the skill executes in a forked subagent context, so its 8,000 tokens of logs land in the subagent rather than the main conversation, and repeated runs stop crowding out the feature work. Option B misreads allowed-tools — it pre-approves the listed tools so they run without permission prompts; it neither reduces output volume nor changes where output goes. Option C misreads argument-hint, which is an autocomplete hint showing expected arguments, not a mechanism that changes skill behavior. Option D only stops Claude from triggering the skill automatically; engineers invoke it deliberately, and each manual run would still dump logs into the main context.

column2:
Your team's /commit skill walks Claude through staging, writing a message, and committing. The team runs it 30-plus times a day in default (Manual) mode, and every run stops three times for approval of git add, git commit, and git status — a flow the team has fully standardized.

What is the most precisely scoped way to remove these prompts?

A. Launch the sessions with --permission-mode bypassPermissions so git commands, along with everything else, never prompt.
B. Add a Bash(*) allow rule to the project's permission settings so no shell command prompts in any session.
C. Add allowed-tools: Bash(git add *) Bash(git commit *) Bash(git status *) to the skill's frontmatter.
D. State in the body of the skill that git add, git commit, and git status are pre-approved and should run without asking.
column3:
Correct Answer: C. Option C scopes the grant to exactly the standardized flow: allowed-tools pre-approves the listed tools for the turn that invokes the skill, so the three prompts disappear only where the team has already decided they add nothing, and the grant clears afterward. Option A removes every permission check in the entire session to fix three prompts — massively over-broad and meant only for isolated environments. Option B permanently pre-approves all shell commands in every context, far beyond the vetted git flow. Option D is prompt-only: permission decisions are made by the permission system, and prose in a skill body cannot grant approval for anything.

References:
• Agent Skills in Claude Code
• Claude Code permissions

column2:
Your /fix-issue skill expects a GitHub issue number and fails early without one. New teammates invoke it bare from the slash menu about half the time, then sit through a failed run before learning that an argument was required.

Which frontmatter addition addresses this?

A. context: fork, so the failed runs at least stay out of the main conversation's context.
B. argument-hint: [issue-number], so autocomplete shows the expected argument when the command is typed.
C. allowed-tools: Bash(gh issue list *), so the skill can enumerate open issues without prompting.
D. A longer description explaining that the skill requires an issue number to run.
column3:
Correct Answer: B. Option B fixes the mistake at the moment it happens: argument-hint is the frontmatter surface shown during autocomplete to indicate expected arguments, so a teammate typing /fix-issue sees [issue-number] before submitting a bare invocation. Option A hides the noise of the failure without preventing the failure. Option C pre-approves an issue-listing command, but a bare invocation still gives the skill no way to know which issue the user meant. Option D puts the requirement in the wrong field — the description exists to convey what the skill does and when it should trigger, and burying an argument requirement there does not surface it at typing time the way the hint does.

• Agent Skills in Claude Code

column2:
Your project CLAUDE.md contains three things: a 60-line release-checklist procedure used about once a week, naming conventions that apply to every file Claude touches, and a rule that Claude must never disable a failing CI check. Overall adherence has been slipping as the file grows.

How should these three items be distributed across instruction surfaces?

A. Checklist into a skill that loads when the task matches; naming conventions stay in CLAUDE.md; the CI rule into a hook that blocks the action.
B. All three into skills, so nothing loads at launch and startup context drops to near zero.
C. All three stay in CLAUDE.md, with the CI rule marked IMPORTANT so it survives the competition for attention.
D. Checklist and the CI rule into .claude/rules/ files path-scoped to release-related directories.
column3:
Correct Answer: A. Option A follows the three-surface split: conventions that apply all the time belong in CLAUDE.md; procedures tied to a kind of task belong in skills, which load only when they apply (only descriptions load until then); and a rule Claude must not be able to skip belongs in a hook, because CLAUDE.md and skills are instructions Claude follows while a hook is code that runs. Option B evicts always-applicable conventions from the one surface designed for them, leaving routine work unguided, and leaves the hard rule skippable. Option C keeps the weekly procedure competing for attention at every launch and leaves a must-never rule dependent on emphasis. Option D misapplies path scoping: the checklist is triggered by a kind of task, not a file location, and the CI rule needs enforcement, not conditional loading.

column2:
Your nightly CI job runs Claude Code headlessly on a shared build server to regenerate API client code; it needs only file reads, edits under src/generated/, and npm run codegen. Twice this month the job hung for its full six-hour timeout because Claude requested approval for a tool nobody anticipated, and no human was there to answer.

Which permission mode should the job use?

A. bypassPermissions, so the job never issues an approval request in the first place.
B. acceptEdits, since the job's work consists mainly of editing generated files.
C. Auto, so a classifier reviews each action and the job proceeds without human approval.
D. dontAsk with the needed tools pre-approved, so anything else is auto-denied instead of prompting.
column3:
Correct Answer: D. Option D is the mode built for unattended pipelines: only pre-approved tools run, and everything else is auto-denied instead of prompting, so the run keeps moving rather than hanging on an approval no one will give — and a codegen job with a small, known toolset loses nothing to the denials. Option A also never prompts, but it skips all permission checks and belongs only inside an isolated container or VM, not on a shared build server. Option B removes prompts for edits only; the next unanticipated command hangs the job again. Option C is the hands-off mode for broader work — it accepts everything subject to classifier review, far more surface than a fixed three-tool job on shared infrastructure needs, when a deterministic allowlist fits exactly.

column2:
Frustrated by approval prompts, an engineer proposes launching every local session with --dangerously-skip-permissions on their laptop, which holds production database credentials and active SSH keys.

What should you advise?

A. Approve it, but add a CLAUDE.md warning telling Claude to be extremely careful around credentials.
B. Reserve bypass for sessions inside an isolated container or VM; on the laptop, run in auto mode instead.
C. Approve it, paired with a Stop hook that runs the full test suite at the end of every turn.
D. Switch the laptop sessions to dontAsk so anything risky is silently denied instead of prompted.
column3:
Correct Answer: B. Option B matches the course's placement of each mode: bypass permissions skips all checks — it is the equivalent of the dangerously-skip flag and belongs only inside an isolated container or VM, not on a machine holding production credentials. Auto mode delivers the prompt relief the engineer wants while a separate classifier reviews each action for intent escalation, such as sending sensitive data to external endpoints or piping downloaded code into a shell. Option A swaps a permission system for a polite request that Claude can fail to follow. Option C checks correctness after the fact; a test suite does nothing to stop a dangerous action from executing. Option D fits unattended pipelines — for interactive development, silent auto-denial of every unlisted tool turns normal exploratory work into a wall of unexplained failures.

column2:
You are setting up four-hour hands-off Claude Code runs for a large migration. The requirements: no permission prompts during the run, dangerous actions such as force pushes and production deploys must be stopped before they execute, and a run must not be allowed to end with a failing test suite.

Which TWO measures together satisfy the requirements? (Select TWO.)

A. Run the sessions in bypassPermissions so nothing interrupts the four-hour window.
B. Run the sessions in auto mode, where a separate classifier reviews each action's intent before it executes.
C. Add a Stop hook that runs the test suite and refuses to let the turn end while tests fail.
D. Add a CLAUDE.md rule requiring Claude to run all tests and to avoid dangerous commands.
column3:
Correct Answer: B and C. Options B and C are the pairing the course teaches for hands-off work, because each covers what the other cannot. Auto mode's classifier guards intent before each action — blocking escalations like force pushes and production deploys — but it never judges correctness, since broken code is not dangerous; it waves broken code through. The Stop hook closes exactly that gap by gating the end of the turn on a passing suite, and it fires whether or not anyone remembers to ask. Option A removes prompts but also removes the pre-execution review the requirements explicitly demand. Option D expresses both requirements as instructions Claude can skip, so neither the danger gate nor the test gate is guaranteed on a run nobody is watching.

column2:
A compliance-sensitive repository requires that an investigation of a proposed dependency upgrade produce a written change proposal while guaranteeing that no file is modified during the investigation. The engineer wants Claude to read the codebase freely without approval prompts slowing the research.

Which permission mode fits?

A. default (Manual), since reads run without prompting and the engineer can decline any edit request.
B. acceptEdits, so the investigation moves quickly and any edits are reviewed after the fact.
C. Plan, where Claude researches in read-only mode and proposes changes without editing anything.
D. Auto, where the classifier reviews each action and blocks any edit the engineer didn't ask for.
column3:
Correct Answer: C. Option C provides the guarantee structurally: plan mode is the read-only mode — Claude reads freely, figures out what needs to change, and hands over a proposal without editing anything, which is exactly the deliverable and the constraint. Option A permits edits whenever the human approves one, so the no-modification guarantee depends on a person catching every prompt correctly. Option B auto-approves file edits — the one action the requirement forbids. Option D guards intent, not read-only-ness: local edits in your own project are precisely the everyday work the classifier waves through, so it guarantees nothing about modification during the investigation.

column2:
You are iterating on a UI prototype, reviewing Claude's work by refreshing the browser after each change. Approval prompts for file edits and routine file-system commands interrupt you roughly 25 times an hour, but you still want anything beyond that — network calls, package installs — to ask first.

Which mode matches this workflow?

A. acceptEdits: reads, file edits, and common file-system commands run without asking, and everything else still prompts.
B. Auto: every action runs without prompting, with a classifier reviewing each one before it executes.
C. bypassPermissions: all checks are skipped so the iteration loop is never interrupted.
D. Plan: Claude proposes each UI change for approval before any file is touched.
column3:
Correct Answer: A. Option A draws the line exactly where you want it: accept edits is the mode for iterating on code you review after the fact — reads, file edits, and common file-system commands run freely, while everything beyond that still asks first. Option B goes further than requested: auto accepts everything, and its classifier waves through precisely the actions (like dependency installs) you said should still prompt. Option C removes all checks, including the ones you explicitly want kept, and belongs only inside isolated containers or VMs. Option D is read-only, so the edit-refresh-review loop cannot happen at all.

column2:
You are kicking off a three-hour refactor before a long meeting and will review the result afterward. You cannot answer prompts while away, the refactor will need commands you cannot fully predict — test runs, dependency installs, git operations on your branch — and you want risky escalations like force pushes stopped before they execute.

Which mode should the session run in?

A. dontAsk, pre-approving the tools you expect the refactor to need so nothing prompts while you are away.
B. acceptEdits, so all the file changes proceed and you review the complete diff after the meeting.
C. default (Manual), queueing the approval prompts so you can answer them all when you return.
D. Auto, where the classifier reviews each action before it runs — blocking escalations while allowing everyday work.
column3:
Correct Answer: D. Option D is the hands-off mode for exactly this job: no prompts interrupt the run, and the separate classifier guards intent — blocking moves that escalate beyond the request, like force pushes, while waving through everyday work such as installing dependencies from the lockfile and pushing to your own branch. Option A is built for unattended pipelines with a known toolset; this job's tool needs are explicitly unpredictable, so the first unanticipated command is auto-denied and the refactor stalls with no one there to notice. Option B still prompts for bash beyond common file-system commands, so the first test run or install leaves the session waiting for an absent human. Option C stalls at the very first non-read action and wastes the entire three-hour window.

column2:
Your monorepo's project CLAUDE.md includes 180 lines of GraphQL-schema conventions that are relevant only to work under src/graphql/. Frontend engineers report that the always-loaded conventions crowd their sessions' context, and adherence to their own rules has dropped as the file grows.

How should the GraphQL conventions be delivered?

A. Keep them in the project CLAUDE.md but move them behind an @ import to a separate graphql-conventions.md file.
B. Move them into the user-level CLAUDE.md of each engineer on the GraphQL team.
C. Move them to .claude/rules/graphql.md with paths: ["src/graphql/**"] in its frontmatter.
D. Convert them into a skill that Claude invokes when it judges that GraphQL work is happening.
column3:
Correct Answer: C. Option C uses the mechanism built for this: a rule file in .claude/rules/ with glob paths frontmatter stays out of context except when Claude is working with matching files, so frontend sessions stop paying for 180 lines they never use while the GraphQL team keeps its conventions in version control for everyone. Option A only reorganizes — imported files are expanded inline at launch, so every session still loads the full content. Option B fragments team-shared conventions into personal files that new engineers will not have and that drift immediately. Option D makes conventions that should always apply to those files contingent on a skill being triggered, where a path-scoped rule loads deterministically whenever matching files are in play.

• Manage Claude's memory (CLAUDE.md)

column2:
Your testing conventions apply to *.test.ts files scattered across 14 packages in a monorepo. A teammate proposes adding a nested CLAUDE.md to each package's test directory so the conventions load only where they apply. You want a solution one person can maintain.

What is the better mechanism?

A. Adopt the proposal: 14 nested CLAUDE.md files, one per package, each loading when Claude reads files in that directory.
B. One .claude/rules/testing.md file with paths: ["**/*.test.ts"] frontmatter, loaded only when Claude works with test files anywhere in the repo.
C. Put the conventions in the root CLAUDE.md marked IMPORTANT so they reliably apply wherever tests are edited.
D. A PreToolUse hook that injects the conventions into context on every edit that touches a .test.ts file.
column3:
Correct Answer: B. Option B fits because the conventions follow a file type, not a location: a path-scoped rule matches by glob pattern, so one maintained file covers every *.test.ts file across all 14 packages and stays out of context the rest of the time. Option A scopes by directory, which forces 14 copies of the same conventions that will drift apart — the maintenance burden you were asked to avoid. Option C pays for the conventions in every session's launch context and spends emphasis on rules that are simply mis-scoped. Option D reaches for enforcement machinery to deliver guidance: hooks are for rules Claude must not be able to skip, and hand-wiring context injection into edit events re-implements what the paths frontmatter already does declaratively.

• Working with large codebases

column2:
Your CLAUDE.md contains the rule IMPORTANT: never run database migrations against the staging database. Across 60 unattended overnight sessions last quarter, Claude ran a staging migration anyway in 3 of them, corrupting shared test data each time.

What is the most effective change?

A. Move the rule to the top of CLAUDE.md and repeat it in the opening prompt of every overnight session.
B. Split CLAUDE.md with imports so the migration rule loads from a small, dedicated rules file.
C. Switch the overnight sessions to a larger model that follows written instructions more reliably.
D. Add a PreToolUse hook that matches migration commands against staging and returns permissionDecision: "deny".
column3:
Correct Answer: D. Option D is correct because CLAUDE.md is guidance Claude usually follows, while a hook is deterministic code that runs at a fixed point in the loop: a PreToolUse deny turns "Claude usually listens" into "Claude can't skip it," which is exactly what a 3-in-60 failure rate on unwatched runs demands. Option A raises emphasis, but emphasis is a budget and the rule remains a probabilistic request. Option B reorganizes the file without changing enforcement; imports are expanded inline and everything still loads as guidance. Option C is the bigger-model anti-pattern: the problem is that prompts cannot guarantee behavior, not that the model is too small.

column2:
You wrote a PreToolUse hook to stop Claude from running terraform apply. The script prints blocked: terraform apply is not allowed to stdout and exits with code 1. In all 12 test sessions, the hook's message appears in the session log, yet Claude still runs terraform apply every time.

Why does the command still run?

A. PreToolUse hooks can only observe tool calls; blocking requires a deny rule in the permission settings instead.
B. The message must be printed to stderr, because stdout is read only after the tool call completes.
C. Exit code 1 is non-blocking; the hook must exit 2, or exit 0 and return JSON with permissionDecision: "deny".
D. The matcher applies only to exact tool names, so Bash commands are never interceptable by PreToolUse.
column3:
Correct Answer: C. Option C is correct: exit code 1 feels like an error but does not block — it is treated as a non-blocking failure, the output is logged, and Claude runs the command anyway. The two blocking paths are exit 2 (with stderr fed back to Claude) or exit 0 with a JSON permissionDecision of deny. Option A is false; PreToolUse is the enforcement primitive and can deny calls before they run. Option B misstates the mechanics: the issue is the exit code, not the output channel. Option D is contradicted by the stem — the hook's message appears in the log, so the matcher already fired on the Bash call.

References:
• Hooks reference
• Get started with hooks

column2:
Your PreToolUse hook redacts sk_live_ secrets from Bash commands by returning updatedInput that contains only the rewritten command field. Since deploying it, redacted commands still run, but three long-running builds failed because the timeout and run_in_background values Claude set on those calls disappeared.

What is causing the lost fields?

A. updatedInput replaces the entire input object, so the hook must echo back every field it is not changing.
B. PreToolUse hooks may modify only one allowlisted field per event; changing command clears the rest by design.
C. Returning updatedInput without an accompanying permissionDecision: "allow" causes unmodified fields to be dropped.
D. The Bash tool re-validates rewritten input and strips any fields the hook did not explicitly approve.
column3:
Correct Answer: A. Option A is correct: updatedInput swaps in a whole new input object rather than patching individual fields, so a hook that returns only command silently discards timeout, run_in_background, and anything else Claude set — the fix is to copy the original input and change just the secret. Option B invents a one-field restriction that does not exist; updatedInput can carry the full object. Option C is wrong because the decision field controls whether the call proceeds, not which fields survive. Option D describes a validation step that does not exist; the fields vanish because the hook's replacement object never included them.

• Get started with hooks

column2:
You are adding a PreToolUse guardrail for kubectl commands in a shared ops repo. Commands against the dev cluster are always fine, commands against prod are never allowed, and commands against staging are legitimate during release weeks but risky otherwise — roughly 20% of staging calls should be stopped, and only the on-call human can tell which.

How should the hook assign its permissionDecision values?

A. allow for dev, deny for prod, and deny for staging with a reason instructing Claude to request approval in chat first.
B. allow for dev, deny for prod, and ask for staging so each staging call is handed to the human to approve or reject.
C. ask for all three clusters so that no kubectl command ever proceeds without a human review.
D. allow for dev and staging, deny for prod, plus a CLAUDE.md note describing when staging commands are risky.
column3:
Correct Answer: B. Option B maps each risk profile to the right decision value: allow for the always-safe case, deny for the never-allowed case, and ask for the genuinely ambiguous case, which is exactly what ask exists for — handing the call back to the user to decide. Option A rebuilds ask out of deny plus a prompt instruction, relying on Claude to voluntarily seek approval instead of using the deterministic mechanism. Option C creates prompt fatigue by forcing review of the 100%-safe dev traffic, which erodes attention for the 20% of staging calls that matter. Option D leaves the risky staging window to prompt guidance, which cannot guarantee the roughly one-in-five calls that must be stopped.

• Get started with hooks

column2:
To keep Claude from writing to infra/prod/, a teammate added a PostToolUse hook on the file-edit tools that exits 2 with the message writes to infra/prod are forbidden. Reviewing a week of session logs, you find 4 sessions in which files under infra/prod/ were modified anyway — each modification followed by the hook's message in the transcript.

Why is the guardrail failing, and what fixes it?

A. Exit code 2 never blocks on any event; the hook must return a JSON decision object instead of relying on exit codes.
B. The message must be written to stdout, because PostToolUse reads stderr only for logging purposes.
C. File-edit tools bypass hooks entirely; the rule must be stated in CLAUDE.md with IMPORTANT emphasis.
D. PostToolUse fires only after the tool call has run, so it cannot prevent the write; the check belongs in PreToolUse, which can deny the call.
column3:
Correct Answer: D. Option D identifies the root cause: PostToolUse runs after a successful tool call, so by the time the hook fires the file is already modified — exit 2 there can only feed the message back to Claude as context, which is what the transcript shows. Moving the path check to PreToolUse lets the hook deny the edit before it happens. Option A is false: exit 2 is the blocking exit code on events that support blocking; the problem is the event's timing, not the mechanism. Option B confuses output channels with blocking behavior. Option C retreats to prompt-only enforcement, which is precisely what a hook is supposed to replace for a hard rule, and file-edit tools do fire hooks.

column2:
Your long refactor sessions compact several times a day. After each compaction, Claude loses track of which of the 14 files in the migration it has already converted and re-edits finished ones, wasting roughly 20 minutes per compaction. You want a short status summary injected into context immediately after every compaction.

Which hook configuration accomplishes this?

A. A PostCompact hook that prints the status summary to stdout.
B. A PreCompact hook that appends the status summary to CLAUDE.md before compaction runs.
C. A SessionStart hook with the compact matcher that prints the summary, which is added back into context.
D. A Stop hook that exits 2 after each compaction until Claude has re-read all 14 files.
column3:
Correct Answer: C. Option C is the pattern the platform supports: to re-inject context after compaction you use SessionStart with the compact matcher — on SessionStart, plain-text stdout is added to context, so the summary lands back in the conversation and Claude resumes where it was. Option A is the common trap: PostCompact fires at the right moment, but its output does not get back into the conversation. Option B mutates a shared guidance file to store transient state, polluting CLAUDE.md for every future session instead of injecting context once. Option D misuses Stop, which fires when Claude tries to end its turn, not at compaction, and forcing 14 file re-reads is exactly the waste you are trying to eliminate.

References:

• Get started with hooks

column2:
In 5 of your last 20 unattended runs, Claude ended its turn declaring the task complete while the test suite was failing; the failures surfaced only the next morning. You want Claude to be unable to end its turn until the suite passes, and to see the failures so it can fix them itself.

Which hook accomplishes this?

A. A PostToolUse hook on file edits that appends each test result to a log file reviewed every morning.
B. A Stop hook that runs the suite and exits 2 with the failure output on stderr when any test fails.
C. A SessionStart hook that injects a reminder that all tests must pass before the turn may end.
D. A PreToolUse hook that denies all further Bash commands once a failing test has been observed.
column3:
Correct Answer: B. Option B uses the event built for this: Stop fires when Claude wants to end its turn, and exit 2 refuses — effectively "no, you're not done" — while feeding the failure output back to Claude as context so it fixes the tests unprompted, on every run, watched or not. Option A preserves the current failure mode: the run still ends green-looking and a human discovers the breakage the next morning. Option C is prompt-only guidance, the same "usually listens" behavior that already failed 5 times in 20 runs. Option D is counterproductive — denying Bash after a failure blocks the very commands Claude needs to run the suite again and fix it.

Domain 1 (Agentic Architecture & Orchestration) · Task 1.4

References:
• Hooks reference
• Claude Code best practices

column2:
Your PostToolUse hook runs the type checker after every edit. Today it writes errors to typecheck.log and exits 0, and engineers find an average of 9 unresolved type errors when they review each finished session. You want Claude to fix type errors as they appear, with no human in the loop.

What change to the hook accomplishes this?

A. Exit 2 and print the type errors to stderr, so they are fed back to Claude as context to act on.
B. Exit 1 and print the type errors to stderr, signaling an error without terminating the session.
C. Keep exit 0 and print the type errors to stdout so Claude parses them automatically.
D. Keep the log file, and add a CLAUDE.md rule telling Claude to read typecheck.log after each edit.
column3:
Correct Answer: A. Option A is the feedback loop hooks are designed for: on PostToolUse, exit 2 feeds stderr straight back to Claude as context, so Claude reads the type errors and fixes them immediately, every run, without anyone asking. Option B fails because exit 1 is non-blocking — the stderr is merely logged and Claude carries on, which is functionally today's behavior. Option C fails because on exit 0 plain text on stdout is ignored on most events (only JSON is parsed; plain text reaches context on events like SessionStart and UserPromptSubmit, not PostToolUse). Option D is prompt-only: Claude will usually remember to read the log, and "usually" is what currently leaves 9 errors per session.

column2:
You are consolidating your team's Claude Code conventions. CLAUDE.md currently holds four rules: (1) never push directly to main; (2) use named exports rather than default exports; (3) never include values matching sk_live_ in any command; (4) write commit messages in the imperative mood. A compliance review found two incidents this quarter in which rules 1 and 3 were violated during unattended sessions.

Which TWO rules should move from CLAUDE.md into hooks? (Select TWO.)

A. Rule 1 — never push directly to main.
B. Rule 2 — use named exports rather than default exports.
C. Rule 3 — never include sk_live_ values in any command.
D. Rule 4 — write commit messages in the imperative mood.
column3:
Correct Answer: A and C. Options A and C are the rules Claude must not be able to skip: both have real compliance consequences, both have already been violated on unattended runs, and both are mechanically checkable — a PreToolUse hook can deny a push to main and can deny or redact a command carrying an sk_live_ secret, turning probabilistic guidance into a guarantee. Options B and D are style conventions where an occasional miss costs a review nit, not an incident; they are exactly what CLAUDE.md guidance is for, and encoding them as hard blocks would add friction without compliance value. The dividing line is the surface model: CLAUDE.md for conventions Claude should follow, hooks for rules it cannot be allowed to break.

column2:
Your release pipeline needs a stage that generates a change summary from the release diff and hands it to the next stage on stdout. The stage runs on an ephemeral CI runner with no TTY, and it must exit as soon as the summary is written.

How should this stage invoke Claude Code?

A. Start an interactive claude session in accept-edits mode and drive it with scripted keystrokes.
B. Invoke claude -p with the diff piped to stdin and the summary written to stdout.
C. Create a routine triggered by an HTTP POST from the pipeline, and have the stage poll for the routine's result.
D. Embed the Agent SDK in a small HTTP service that the pipeline stage calls for each release.
column3:
Correct Answer: B. Option B is what headless mode is for: -p (alias --print) runs Claude Code as a one-shot, non-interactive command that reads stdin and writes stdout, so it composes with the pipeline like any other shell tool and exits when done. Option A depends on an interactive TUI on a runner with no TTY and is brittle by construction. Option C moves the work onto Anthropic's managed infrastructure, so the result never lands on this stage's stdout and the stage gains a polling loop it does not need. Option D is over-engineered — the SDK earns its keep when Claude Code belongs inside your own product, not for a single pipeline stage a one-line command can serve.

column2:
A nightly headless job asks Claude to list deprecated API calls per file, and a downstream script parses the prose response. The parse step breaks in about 15% of runs because the format drifts — sometimes bullets, sometimes a table, sometimes a paragraph.

What is the most reliable fix?

A. Add "Respond ONLY with a JSON array and no prose" to the prompt, and retry the run whenever parsing fails.
B. Rewrite the parser as a more tolerant set of regexes that accepts bullets, tables, and paragraphs.
C. Add a second claude -p call that converts the first run's prose into JSON before the script reads it.
D. Pass --output-format json with a --json-schema, and have the script read the result from the structured_output field.
column3:
Correct Answer: D. Option D removes the failure mode instead of coping with it: pairing a JSON schema with JSON output constrains Claude's answer to your schema, and the conforming object lands in structured_output, ready to pull with jq into the next step. Option A is prompt-only compliance — mostly honored, which is exactly how you get a 15% breakage rate — and retries burn pipeline minutes without guaranteeing a parse. Option B hardens the parser against the formats seen so far while leaving it exposed to the next drift. Option C adds a second model invocation to translate output the first invocation could have produced correctly, doubling cost and adding a new place to fail.

column2:
The same claude -p audit command behaves differently across CI runners and laptops: on some machines it triggers a teammate's ~/.claude PreToolUse hooks, and in one project it connected to the MCP servers in the repo's .mcp.json, adding about 40 seconds of startup. You want every machine to run the identical minimal environment — Claude plus only the tools the script allows explicitly.

What change achieves this?

A. Add --bare to the command, which skips auto-discovery of hooks, skills, plugins, MCP servers, and CLAUDE.md.
B. Add a setup step that deletes ~/.claude and the repo's .mcp.json on each machine before the audit runs.
C. Pin the same model version in every environment so all runs behave identically.
D. Build a container image containing an approved CLAUDE.md and run the audit inside it on every machine.
column3:
Correct Answer: A. Option A is the built-in answer: --bare skips auto-discovery of hooks, skills, plugins, MCP servers, and CLAUDE.md, giving you Claude plus only what the script explicitly allows — the same result on every machine, with faster startup, which is exactly the deterministic behavior CI wants. Option B destroys developers' personal configuration and repo files to simulate what a flag already does, and must be maintained on every machine forever. Option C addresses model behavior, not the real variable — what each machine's environment loads. Option D is over-engineered: standing up container infrastructure to approximate a CLI flag, and whatever configuration ends up in the image is still auto-discovered inside it.

column2:
Your migration automation runs in two stages: at 02:00 a headless run analyzes the codebase and produces a migration plan, and at 04:00 — after a database snapshot completes — a second headless run must execute that plan with full awareness of the analysis, including which files were examined and which approaches were ruled out.

How should the second stage obtain that context?

A. Include the first run's final plan text in the second run's prompt.
B. Combine both stages into one -p invocation that sleeps for two hours between analysis and execution.
C. Capture the session_id from the first run's JSON output and start the second stage with --resume.
D. Save the first run's full transcript to a file and have the second run load it using a larger context window.
column3:
Correct Answer: C. Option C is the multi-step automation pattern headless mode supports: the JSON output carries the session ID, and resuming that session at 04:00 restores the full working context — the files examined, the dead ends ruled out, and the plan — so the executor picks up exactly where the analyzer stopped. Option A carries only the plan artifact; the reasoning behind it, which the stem says the executor needs, is lost. Option B holds a runner hostage for two hours and breaks the one-shot semantics of -p, and any failure in the window loses both stages. Option D is the bigger-context anti-pattern: re-ingesting a raw transcript is an expensive, lossy reconstruction of state that --resume restores directly.

column2:
You want a dependency audit to run against your repo every morning at 9am and open a PR when patched versions are available. The team has no CI set up for this repo, nobody wants to maintain a workflow file, and no machine can be left running.

Which approach fits these constraints best?

A. Create a routine with /schedule so the job runs on Anthropic's managed infrastructure.
B. Add a GitHub Actions workflow with a 9am cron trigger that invokes claude -p and opens the PR.
C. Run a cron job on a team member's laptop that invokes claude -p at 9am and opens the PR with gh.
D. Build a small scheduler service on the Agent SDK, deploy it to your cloud account, and have it run the audit at 9am.
column3:
Correct Answer: A. Option A matches every constraint: a routine bundles a prompt, the repository, and any connectors, and runs on a cron trigger on Anthropic's managed infrastructure — no machine of yours stays on and no workflow file exists to maintain. Recurring, same-prompt work like a morning dependency audit is the canonical routine use case. Option B satisfies the schedule but reintroduces exactly the workflow file the team refuses to own. Option C depends on a laptop being awake and online at 9am every day. Option D is the maximum-effort end of the spectrum — building and hosting a service — for a job whose defining property is that nothing should be built or hosted.

column2:
Your nightly routine is prompted to "fix one flaky test, push the fix to main, and carry over notes from the previous night's run." After two weeks you observe: main has zero commits from the routine, its pushes all appear on branches named claude/..., and every night's run re-diagnoses the flakiness from scratch as if the earlier runs never happened.

Which explanation matches this behavior?

A. The routine's GitHub connector was created without write access, so its pushes are being redirected to scratch branches.
B. Each routine run starts from a fresh clone of the default branch and can push only to claude/-prefixed branches unless that guardrail is loosened for the repo.
C. Routine pushes to protected branches are queued for manual approval and are waiting in the routine dashboard.
D. Overnight compaction dropped both the push instruction and the previous night's notes from the routine's context.
column3:
Correct Answer: B. Option B describes the designed guardrails: every routine run begins from a fresh clone of the default branch — which is why no state or notes persist between nights — and pushes are restricted to claude/-prefixed branches unless you loosen that per repo, which is the safeguard keeping an autonomous run from rewriting main. Both observed symptoms follow from this one design. Option A is contradicted by the stem: pushes are landing successfully, so write access exists. Option C invents an approval queue routines do not have. Option D misattributes a persistent, by-design behavior to compaction, and compaction within one run would not explain fourteen consecutive nights of identical amnesia.

column2:
After each production deploy completes — at unpredictable times, 3 to 8 times a day — you want a routine to scan the new Sentry errors and file a triage summary. Deploys are driven by an internal release system, not by GitHub.

How should the routine be triggered?

A. An hourly cron schedule, accepting up to an hour of delay after each deploy.
B. A GitHub event trigger on pushes to the release branch, since each deploy corresponds to a release push.
C. A SessionStart hook in the repo that launches the scan whenever a session begins.
D. An HTTP POST from the release system to the routine's API endpoint after each deploy.
column3:
Correct Answer: D. Option D uses the trigger built for this: routines fire on a cron schedule, a GitHub event, or an HTTP POST to their API endpoint, and only the internal release system knows the moment a deploy completes — one POST at that moment gives immediate, exactly-per-deploy runs. Option A turns an event into polling: up to an hour of latency per incident and wasted runs during deploy-free hours. Option B fires at the wrong moment — a push to the release branch is not deploy completion, and the stem says deploys are driven by the internal release system, not GitHub. Option C is a category error: hooks run at fixed points inside a Claude Code session; they are not an external scheduler, and no session is running when the deploy lands.

column2:
Your 8-person team wants every pull request in three repos reviewed by Claude, with findings posted as inline comments on the changed lines and tagged by severity. Nobody wants to build or host anything, and your organization is on an Enterprise plan.

What is the most direct path?

A. Write a review workflow in each repo using anthropics/claude-code-action@v1 with a custom review prompt.
B. Have an org admin enable Code Review from the Claude Code admin settings, install the Claude GitHub app, and pick the three repos and when reviews run.
C. Ask every engineer to run /code-review locally before opening a pull request.
D. Create a routine per repo, triggered on new pull requests, that posts its findings as a PR comment.
column3:
Correct Answer: B. Option B is the managed path built for exactly this: an Anthropic-hosted service, enabled by an org admin, that reviews PRs through the Claude GitHub app and posts inline, severity-tagged findings — deduplicated and ranked — with nothing for the team to build or host. Option A wires up custom CI to reproduce what the managed service already does, and now three workflows must be maintained. Option C is manual and unenforced — it depends on each engineer remembering, and the findings never appear as inline comments on the PR for reviewers. Option D rebuilds review on routine infrastructure without the managed service's review pipeline, and a single rolled-up comment is not inline findings on changed lines.

column2:
Beyond review comments, your team wants this behavior: when a developer comments @claude implement the spec in the linked issue on a pull request, Claude should push commits to that PR's branch and post a comment describing what it did. Managed Code Review is already enabled on the repo.

What should you add?

A. Nothing new — configure managed Code Review's @claude review trigger to also apply the changes it suggests.
B. A routine with a GitHub trigger on PR comments that implements the spec.
C. A workflow using anthropics/claude-code-action@v1, set up via /install-github-app, listening for the @claude trigger phrase.
D. A Stop hook in the repo that implements the linked spec whenever a review session finishes.
column3:
Correct Answer: C. Option C is the do-it-yourself path for jobs that go beyond review: the GitHub Action runs the agent on PR and issue comments, so an @claude mention (the default trigger_phrase) kicks off a run that pushes commits and posts comments — exactly the requested behavior — and /install-github-app handles app installation and the API key secret. Option A misreads the managed service's boundaries: it posts findings only, never applies changes, and never approves or blocks. Option B collides with routine guardrails — each run starts from a fresh clone of the default branch and pushes only to claude/-prefixed branches, not the PR's own branch. Option D is a category error: hooks fire inside a local session's loop, not in response to GitHub comment events.

column2:
Your scheduled repository-report workflow uses anthropics/claude-code-action@v1. Last month it hung twice for the full 6-hour job timeout waiting on a permission prompt no one would ever answer, and once it looped for 47 turns before the job was killed. The report only needs to read the repo and post one comment.

Which TWO configuration changes best fix these failures? (Select TWO.)

A. Raise the workflow's timeout-minutes so a permission prompt has more time to be answered.
B. Pass --permission-mode dontAsk through claude_args so tools that are not pre-approved are auto-denied instead of prompting.
C. Pre-approve every tool so that no action ever needs permission.
D. Cap the agent loop by passing --max-turns through claude_args.
column3:
Correct Answer: B and D. Option B fixes the hangs at the root: in an unattended pipeline there is no one to answer a prompt, and dontAsk auto-denies anything not pre-approved instead of waiting, so the run can never stall on an approval. Option D fixes the runaway: a --max-turns cap in claude_args puts a hard ceiling on the agent loop, ending the 47-turn spiral deterministically. Option A extends the hang rather than curing it — the prompt will still never be answered, just for more billable minutes. Option C trades the hang for unbounded privilege: a read-only report should be scoped to read-only tools, and blanket approval does nothing about looping.

column2:
You wired your own PR-review workflow with claude-code-action@v1, running on every push. Active PRs average 6 pushes, and by merge time each carries roughly 40 review comments — mostly the same findings re-posted by later runs, plus dozens of style nits. Reviewers have started ignoring the bot, but the team wants every push to keep being reviewed.

What is the most effective change?

A. Replace the workflow with managed Code Review, which deduplicates and ranks findings across pushes.
B. Add "do not repeat findings already posted by earlier runs, and skip style nits" to the workflow's review prompt.
C. Trigger the review only when the PR is opened or marked ready for review, so each PR is commented on exactly once.
D. Cap the workflow at five comments per run, ordered by the model's own severity rating, so the total volume stays manageable.
column3:
Correct Answer: A. Option A fixes both symptoms with the service designed for them: the managed review pipeline deduplicates and ranks findings by severity, so reviewers read a short list of real issues rather than a wall of repeats and nits, while still reviewing ongoing pushes. Option B is prompt-only enforcement aimed at an instance that cannot comply — each workflow run is a fresh instance with no memory of what earlier runs posted, so it has nothing to check the instruction against. Option C removes duplication by abandoning the stated requirement that every push stays reviewed. Option D is an arbitrary cap: five comments per run still repeat the same findings across the 6 runs, and a per-run self-rating is no substitute for deduplication across runs.

column2:
Your automation pipeline has one Claude instance implement a change from an issue, then a separate fresh instance review the resulting PR. A teammate proposes feeding the implementer's session transcript into the review run "so the reviewer understands the intent and stops flagging things the implementer already considered."

How should you respond to the proposal?

A. Accept it, but pass a condensed summary of the transcript instead of the full text to save tokens.
B. Reject it, because implementation transcripts are too large to fit in the review run's context window.
C. Accept it, because a reviewer that knows the intent will produce fewer false-positive findings.
D. Reject it: a reviewer with no memory of how the code was built catches what the implementation run talked itself past.
column3:
Correct Answer: D. Option D preserves the property that makes the second instance valuable: fresh context. A cold reviewer judges the code on its own merits, so the rationalizations the implementer "already considered" get re-tested instead of inherited — that is precisely how it catches what the original run talked itself past. Option A imports the implementer's framing in condensed form, recreating the same blind spots at lower token cost. Option B rejects for the wrong reason; the principle is independence, not context size, and a summary would fit anyway. Option C is the trap in the proposal itself: the findings suppressed as "already considered" are exactly the ones an independent review exists to surface.

column2:
An unattended overnight run reports: "Refactored the payment retry logic in src/billing/retry.ts; all 214 tests pass." CI independently ran the full suite and is green. You have 15 minutes before standup to decide whether this is ready for a pull request.

Where should you spend those 15 minutes first?

A. The run's summary, cross-checking each file and test count it names against the repository state.
B. The session transcript, replaying Claude's reasoning and tool calls from the beginning of the run.
C. The diff itself, via /code-review and then git diff, checking for changes outside the planned files.
D. A fresh session's opinion on whether the summary and the CI result together sound complete and plausible.
column3:
Correct Answer: C. Option C follows the core rule for unsupervised work: start from the diff, not the summary. The trap is a tidy write-up that reads fine while the diff quietly touched files you did not expect; /code-review flags issues and your own pass over git diff — planned files first, then anything outside the plan — is what exposes scope surprises, the one risk the green test suite does not cover. Option A is bounded by what the summary chooses to mention, which is exactly the untrusted artifact. Option B narrates intent step by step and will not fit a 15-minute window; effects live in the diff. Option D asks a model to review prose about the code rather than the code, so an omission in the summary survives the check.

column2:
After a 3-hour unsupervised run produced a large diff, you asked the same session to "critically review your own work." It reported zero issues. A human skim later found a subtle concurrency bug in code the session had rewritten twice during the run.

Which review setup would most likely have caught the bug?

A. Asking the original session to review again with stronger wording, such as "be extremely critical this time."
B. Having the original session rate its confidence per file, then reviewing only the files rated below 80%.
C. Re-running the entire task in a second session and diffing the two resulting implementations.
D. Having a fresh session or subagent review the diff with no memory of how the code was built.
column3:
Correct Answer: D. Option D is the cold second opinion: a reviewer with no memory of the run has no stake in the approach, so the reasoning that talked the original session past the concurrency bug — twice — carries no weight with it, and the code is judged on what it actually does. Option A adds emphasis but keeps the same stakeholder; the blind spot that produced the bug also hides it from self-review. Option B routes attention by self-reported confidence, an unreliable signal — the session was confident enough to rewrite that code twice and report zero issues. Option C is over-engineered: two divergent implementations produce a wall of incidental differences that localizes nothing, at double the cost of simply reviewing the diff that exists.

column2:
A nightly headless job runs claude -p across 30 repos to apply a dependency bump, and you have about 20 minutes each morning to triage. Today you skim all 30 prose outputs, which consumes the whole window and has still missed 2 failed runs this month.

What triage process should replace this?

A. Check each run's exit code and JSON result first, then spend the window on the failures plus a sample of passing runs' diffs.
B. Pipe all 30 outputs into a single Claude session and read its combined summary of what succeeded and failed.
C. Have each run append a self-assessed confidence percentage and read only the runs scoring below 80%.
D. Drop the morning triage and investigate only the repos whose CI breaks later in the day.
column3:
Correct Answer: A. Option A applies the rule for headless work — verify runs by their JSON result and exit code. Those signals are machine-checkable, so the 2 failures this month would surface in seconds instead of being lost in prose, and the reclaimed time goes where judgment matters: the failing runs plus a rotating sample of passing diffs, which is how trust in the other 28 is earned rather than assumed. Option B trades 30 summaries for a summary of summaries — the same trust-the-prose failure mode, aggregated. Option C routes attention by self-reported confidence, which is not a reliable escalation signal. Option D is purely reactive: regressions ship and CI becomes your users' first reviewer.

column2:
Your team is scaling unattended auto-mode runs from 5 to 40 per week. Verification today is: read Claude's summary, and trust that auto mode's classifier reviewed each action. Two regressions shipped last month from runs whose summaries claimed "all tests pass."

Which TWO changes would give these runs real verification? (Select TWO.)

A. Wire the test suite as a Stop hook that refuses to end the turn on failure, so tests actually run and gate every session.
B. Keep relying on the auto-mode classifier, but configure it more strictly, since it already reviews every action.
C. Require each run's summary to quote the test command and its full output verbatim.
D. Add a fresh-context review of each run's diff before anything merges.
column3:
Correct Answer: A and D. Option A turns tests from a claim into a gate: the Stop hook runs the suite itself and refuses to end the turn on failure, so "all tests pass" can no longer be asserted without being true, and the exit-2 feedback lets Claude fix failures unprompted — closing the exact hole behind last month's regressions. Option D adds the cold second opinion: a fresh-context reviewer of the diff has no stake in the approach and catches what the run talked itself past, which matters most when nobody watched the run. Option B misunderstands the classifier: it guards dangerous actions and never judges correctness, so no strictness setting makes it catch broken code. Option C is still self-reported — a summary is authored by the same run being verified, and quoted output can be stale or wrong with nobody checking it.

column2:
A teammate installed a community-marketplace plugin for its SQL-formatting skill. A week later you notice that every session in that project makes an outbound network request each time Claude ends its turn. Nothing in your own .claude configuration references that endpoint.

What explains the requests, and what should have happened before installing?

A. Claude Code telemetry makes the calls; the community marketplace's automated review would have flagged anything else before publication.
B. Plugins execute in a sandbox that cannot reach the network, so an MCP server configured in the project must be responsible.
C. The plugin bundled a Stop hook that now fires alongside your own configuration on every turn; its hooks, agents, and MCP servers should have been reviewed before install.
D. Installing a plugin for one skill installs only that skill, so someone must have added the network hook to the project separately.
column3:
Correct Answer: C. Option C matches both the symptom and the lesson: a plugin is one installable unit, so installing it for a skill also installs its hooks — a bundled Stop hook fires on every turn, stacking alongside your own hooks rather than appearing in your configuration — and a plugin runs code on your machine with your privileges, which is why reading its components before install is the rule. Option A leans on automated review as a guarantee, but reviewed is not the same as trusted — automated review catches some things, not everything, and it does not explain a turn-end request pattern. Option B invents a network sandbox plugins do not have. Option D gets the bundling model backwards: you get every component the plugin ships, whether you wanted it or not.

column2:
Your platform team's .claude setup — 6 skills, 2 subagents, a hooks file, and an MCP config — works well. Thirty engineers across 12 repos currently copy the folder around by hand; after the latest update, 11 of them were found still running a version with a broken hook that had been fixed three weeks earlier.

What distribution approach fixes this?

A. Commit the .claude folder to a template repository that engineers copy when creating new projects.
B. Package the setup as a plugin and add a private marketplace, so every engineer installs and updates through one versioned source.
C. Merge the six skills' contents into a shared CLAUDE.md that is redistributed whenever it changes.
D. Have each engineer maintain a personal fork of the folder and cherry-pick fixes as they land.
column3:
Correct Answer: B. Option B is what plugins are for: the existing .claude shape packages as-is into one installable unit — skills, subagents, hooks, and MCP config — and a private marketplace added once (/plugin marketplace add) gives centralized discovery, version tracking, and updates, so the 11 stale copies become a version bump instead of a hunt across laptops. Option A helps only at project creation; the 12 existing repos keep drifting exactly as they do today. Option C moves task-scoped procedures onto the always-loaded guidance surface — every line now competes for attention in every session — and the distribution problem remains manual. Option D makes drift the design: 30 forks cherry-picking independently is how the broken-hook situation happened.
